Grading Method
Tags: courses
Short Description: The method used to assign grades for a course, such as letter grades or S/U.
Grading Method

A grading method in which student performance is evaluated using letter grades from A (Superior) through F (Failure), with each grade assigned a quality point value used to calculate GPA.
8.53.10 Student grades are defined as follows: A – Superior B – Good C – Fair D – Low grade, passing F – Failure 8.53.11 Grades shall be given quality point values as follows: A = 4.00 points A- = 3.70 points B+ = 3.30 points B = 3.00 points B- = 2.70 points C+ = 2.30 points C = 2.00 points C- = 1.70 points D+ = 1.30 points D = 1.00 points F = 0 points U = 0 points U* = not calculated in GPA

Certain courses do not lend themselves to precise grading. For these courses, only S (satisfactory) or U (unsatisfactory) is given to all students enrolled. S/U courses are labeled as such in the course descriptions in this catalog. S/U courses are not counted as courses taken under the Pass-Fail option.
D1 is the only General Education outcome that can be graded using S/U or Letter Grades. All other outcomes must be graded by Letter Grades.

Tags: courses,programs,specializations
Short Description: Proposers should review existing curricula and ensure that proposed courses, programs, and specializations do not contain substantial content overlap.
Content Overlap
Proposed courses, programs, and specializations are reviewed for potential content overlap with existing curricula. Proposers should review existing curricula and ensure that proposed courses, programs, and specializations do not contain substantial actual or perceived content overlap.
Early consultation with potentially affected academic units may help identify concerns, clarify distinctions between offerings, and support an efficient review process.
A letter of support, which may be provided as an email from an affected department chair, can be uploaded to the Kuali proposal to document (a) that both departments have considered potential content overlap; (b) communication between the affected department and the department proposing the curriculum; and (c) the affected department’s support for the proposed curriculum.

Course Description
Tags: courses
Short Description: Student-facing summary of a course that clearly and concisely communicates its content, purpose, and focus.
Course Description
Course descriptions are written for students, not faculty, and must communicate clearly and concisely to them. Jargon, acronyms, and technical language should be avoided as much as possible. Anyone should be able to read the description and understand the nature and intent of the course.
An acceptable course description with a maximum of 30 words, begins with a verb, e.g. examines, introduces, explores, investigates. Articles, adjectives and adverbs are seldom necessary. Sentence fragments are acceptable.

Course Number
Tags: courses
Short Description: The numerical portion of a course identifier that follows the Subject Code (e.g., ENG101, where ENG is the Subject Code and 101 is the Course Number).
Course Number

Pre-freshman and special undergraduate. Characteristics: Undergraduate courses not applicable for degree credit. Post-Secondary or sub-freshman remedial courses, Alan Shawn Feinstein College of Education and Professional Studies courses for no credit or for non-credit certificate credit only.

Lower division undergraduate courses. Primarily for freshmen and sophomores and as electives for upper class students. Characteristics: Little or no prior college level work required. May not be taken for graduate credit.

Upper division undergraduate courses. Primarily for juniors and seniors majoring in the field or advanced students in other disciplines. Characteristics: Some formal background or sophistication required but not to the extent that would ordinarily justify allowing graduate degree credit.

Generally limited to juniors and seniors majoring in the field. Open to other advanced undergraduates and to graduate students with permission. Characteristics: Extensive background required, may be taken for graduate credit. (Limitations may be stated by the department if desired.)
Courses numbered at the 400 level that are available for graduate credit must be approved by both the appropriate Undergraduate Curriculum Committee (CASC or GEC) and the Graduate Council.

Graduate level courses. The bachelor’s degree is usually a prerequisite but qualified seniors and honors students can be admitted with permission. Characteristics: Comprise majority of course work between bachelor’s and master’s degree. Number 599 reserved for masters thesis research and is graded on an S/U-only basis.

Advanced graduate courses. No undergraduates admitted except honors students with approval of advisors and the department. Characteristics: Comprise majority of course work between master’s and doctor’s degree but not limited to doctoral students. Number 699 reserved for doctoral thesis research and is graded on an S/U-only basis.

Special types of graduate courses for which no program credit is allowed. Characteristics: Workshops, institutes, courses taken for certificate credit only, courses taken to remedy deficiencies, and temporary courses which have not been approved by the Graduate Council for graduate program credit.
